questions.question: Which data structure is optimized for extremely fast 'have we seen this before?' checks, with no duplicates and no guaranteed order?
questions.explanation: A set stores unique values and is specifically optimized for fast membership checks, unlike a list which may need to check every item one by one.

questions.question: Why does checking whether an item exists in a list get slower as the list grows, while a set or dictionary lookup stays roughly constant?
options: Lists are stored on a slower part of the computer's memory
A list search may need to check every item one by one (linear search), while sets and dictionaries use a lookup method that doesn't depend on the total size
Sets and dictionaries are written in a faster programming language
Lists can only hold 1,000 items maximum
questions.explanation: A list's 'is this in here?' check is a linear search that can require scanning every element, so time grows with list size. Sets and dictionaries use hashing to find items almost instantly regardless of size.

questions.question: Engineering says a permissions lookup went from 5 minutes to instant by 'switching from a list to a dictionary.' Which question best confirms this fix generalizes and isn't a one-off?
options: Can we just add more servers instead?
As this dataset grows 10x or 100x further, will this lookup's speed stay roughly the same, or will it degrade again?
Why was a list used at all if dictionaries exist?
Can we remove the permissions check entirely?
questions.explanation: Confirming the fix generalizes as data scales is the key follow-up — dictionary/set lookups stay fast regardless of size, so this should hold even as the dataset grows further, unlike the original list-based linear search.
